label: General MIDI standard drum kit, close mics, dry
_takes: A kit fitted one hit at a time has no measurement of what happens between hits, and that is where a drum part lives: the hi-hats share a GM exclusive class, so striking one chokes the others, and the single-hit probe strikes one note every two seconds and has never fired it. The phrase set is what the ear checks that against.
audition_title: libsonare drum kit vs the sampled reference
_channel: Channel 10 (9 zero-based) is what makes a note number select an instrument instead of a pitch, on the reference as much as in libsonare. A drum sampler that answers on any channel will still record correctly here; a GM-conformant reference will record a piano if this is left off, and the corpus would look like a successful capture of the wrong instrument.
_dry: Close mics with the plugin's room and bus sections off. A kit is the one percussion case where dry is both achievable and wanted: the ambience is a mix decision rather than part of the instrument, and libsonare's own send weighting is fitted separately. If the reference cannot be dried - some kits bake the overheads into every sample - clear `dry` and let the room correction handle it, the same way the organ capture does. Here it was achieved: `calibrate` measures RT60 0.00 s, against 3.14 s on the organ capture, so the switch reached what it advertised.
_calibration: From `capture.py calibrate`: the reference renders identically in real time and faster than it, and the measured settle minimum is 250 ms. `realtime` is on anyway, and the reason is a measurement rather than caution. Rendering this grid with it off failed 63 of 282 notes - the sampler returned digital silence and the retry found it five times running - and the failures were not the exotic notes but the snare, the closed hi-hat and the ride. So `calibrate` measuring real time as optional says only that one note on an otherwise idle machine did not need it; a 282-note grid streaming from disk, on a machine doing anything else at the same time, does. Read that recipe line as the floor it is.
_stimulus: 50 ms, because on a drum channel the note-off carries no information: a kit's percussion is voiced as a one-shot and renders identically at any gate. Measured rather than assumed, on the three notes that would show a choke first - open hi-hat, ride and crash, rendered at 50, 250 and 1000 ms - and the RMS agrees to inside 0.1 dB in every window out to two seconds. Worth measuring because the failure is silent: a kit that did choke would fill the corpus with short cymbals and nothing downstream would report anything but a successful capture. The remaining exceptions are the notes a kit voices as held instruments - typically the whistles and the record scratches - whose length is whatever the gate was on the reference side and a constant on the model side. Fitting one of those means re-capturing it at a longer gate, not reading its envelope from this grid.
_tail_by_note: The cymbals need a longer recording than the rest of the kit, and measuring the difference is what says so. At a 2s tail every cymbal's `decay_ms` in reference/drums.json - the time to fall 20 dB - sat between 1170 and 1760 ms against an analysis ceiling of 1800, and five rows were flagged `decay_capped`: those numbers were the window and not the instrument. Recorded to 8s and analysed to `HIT_LONG_MAX_SEC`, nothing is capped and the numbers move where they had been pinned - ride 1 to 2056 ms, crash 2 to 2007, open triangle from 1220 to 2245 - while every cymbal that had room already reads within a few ms of what it did. A flat 8s tail would triple the whole 282-note grid's render time for the sake of ten notes; naming them costs about six minutes. 49-59 covers every cymbal and the ride bell, and is written as a range rather than as the cymbal list, so 50, 54, 56 and 58 are recorded long as well; that costs a few minutes and is cheaper than a hand-kept list that has to stay in step with GM's numbering. 80-81 is the triangle pair. `metrics.LONG_DECAY_DRUM_NOTES` also names 84, the belltree, and this deliberately does not: that set is a fact about instruments, while this grid is the GM standard kit and stops at 81, so a tail entry for 84 would read as a decision and record nothing. That criterion is the time to fall 20 dB, and it is not the only one the grid has to satisfy. `density` and `prompt` are gated on the recording's own noise floor, which needs the piece to fall 60 dB and then stay there long enough to read one - so a piece can be recorded well past its `decay_ms` and still have no floor. The open hi-hat was: at the kit's 2s its tail ended 17 to 39 dB per band above its own lead-in, plainly still sounding, and both terms were refused for it. 46 is named at 5s for that and reaches a floor 2.1 s in, which takes `shape score` from 31 of 45 note-and-layer pairs to 35. None of that moved a single row of reference/drums.json, because every dimension `profile.py` measures stops at its analysis ceiling well before the new tail begins; the length is bought for the floor-gated terms alone. Ride 1 and ride 2 are still open. They are inside 49-59 and still ringing at the end of the 8s, and extrapolating their late slope they need about 18s to fall 60 dB - which is not a per-note cost, because the analysis plane is sized to the LONGEST slot in the grid and every note is padded to it. Recording those two long makes every spectrogram in the harness 2.5 times the size, so it is a decision about the whole grid rather than about two notes.
_round_robin: A sampled kit commonly alternates between several recordings of the same strike, which makes the reference non-deterministic in a way that reads as measurement noise in every metric. `capture.py calibrate` renders the same note twice and reports whether the two agree; check that before trusting a corpus, because a round robin left on puts a floor under the loss that no knob can go below. This kit has none: re-rendering 120 slots of the grid reproduced every good one bit for bit, and a loss that stops falling has stopped for a reason worth finding. What that same re-render did find is a different thing entirely, and calibrate's one note could never have shown it - see `_late_renders`.
_late_renders: A render can come back loud, plausible, and not the note. Re-rendering 120 slots and correlating against the originals, 39 of them returned a completely different signal - correlation 0.000, 4 to 25 dB LOUDER than the real note, beginning 150 to 843 ms into the file after a stretch of digital silence, where every correct render begins at exactly the 100 ms preroll. Whole instruments were affected: all six velocities of the closed hi-hat and of the mute triangle, whose peak levels then read -7.99, -8.03, -8.04, -0.57, -0.79, -0.32 dBFS against a clean ramp that ascends smoothly. Being loud is why nothing caught it - the capture's retry asks whether the samples arrived, and these arrived, late and wrong. `capture.py` now also asks WHEN, retries a render whose audio starts more than `ONSET_SLACK_MS` past the preroll, and records `onset_ms` per slot so the manifest can be audited. Any measurement taken from this kit before that guard existed is suspect, and the whole grid was recaptured under it.
_timbres: One kit per timbre, on its own channel slot if the plugin is a rack. Two rather than one because a single reference has no spread, and without a spread no dimension can be judged against anything: a gate written from one kit holds the model to that kit's mixing decisions as if they were the instrument's properties. The second is named for what was measured rather than for a product, because the rack publishes no slot names and a label claiming one would be the single unverifiable line in a file whose point is that its contents were measured. Selected against the fourteen percussion slots the rack turned out to hold: `kit-b` answers the whole General MIDI map with a General MIDI layout (a kick low, a bright closed hat, a crash that rings), which the slots reading a 50 Hz kick or a 250 Hz note 42 do not, and it sits far enough from `kit-a` to be a different instrument rather than the same one processed differently. Its near neighbours in the rack were deliberately NOT taken as a third: two kits a couple of decibels apart would put the spread where the gate's discriminating power is supposed to be, which is a gate that passes because its references agree.

timbres.label: Second kit: deeper kick and floor tom, brighter closed hat

_notes: The General MIDI standard kit, note 35 to note 81, every instrument in it. A drum fit is per-note - each instrument is its own patch, or shares one with its neighbours - so there is no register to interpolate across and no note that another note stands in for.
_toms: The six tom keys do NOT hold the pitch order General MIDI names them in, so a tom fit scored against this capture note-for-note fits the wrong drum. Measured fundamentals, consistent across every velocity: note 45 at 72 Hz, 47 at 79, 48 at 92, 50 at 97, 41 at 170, 43 at 188. That is a clean ascending series of six toms laid out as 45, 47, 48, 50, 41, 43 - the two smallest toms sit on the low-floor-tom keys, where GM puts the two largest. libsonare's own toms key-track, so they run 100 to 167 Hz in note order and no single key pairs with its reference row: 41 and 43 read 0.6x the reference and 45 through 50 read 1.6-1.9x. Every other family in this capture does follow GM - the hats, snares and cymbals were identified by their band profiles and fitted against these rows - so this is a property of the six tom keys and not of the capture. Nothing here is wrong as a measurement; the rows are correct for the keys they were struck on. What is blocked is reading a tom disagreement as a voicing error.
_note_map: The six tom keys do not hold the pitch order General MIDI names them in, so a tom fit scored against this capture note-for-note fits the wrong drum. `note_map` pairs each captured note with the model note of the same rank, and is applied to the oracle side only: libsonare ships GM's layout because that is what a MIDI file is written against, and correcting the model would calibrate this reference's idiosyncrasy into the product. Median measured fundamentals: note 45 at 72 Hz, 47 at 79, 48 at 92, 50 at 97, 41 at 170, 43 at 188 - one clean ascending series of six toms laid out as 45, 47, 48, 50, 41, 43, with the two largest on the keys where GM puts the two smallest. Every other family here does follow GM: the hats, snares and cymbals were identified by their band profiles and fitted against these rows unmapped.
_groups: Which of these notes are one instrument. A kit is not 47 independent objects: six toms are one series of sizes, three hi-hats are one mechanism at three openings, a mute and an open cuica are one drum played two ways, and every per-hit metric in the harness is taken against that hit's own reference row and can say nothing about the relation. `loss._kit_terms` scores it, as the sorted contrasts within each family, so a family is a SET and needs neither an order nor the note map - the toms group correctly whichever key holds which drum. Which relations a family actually holds is measured from the rows rather than declared here, and the rows say all thirteen hold several: median spread across the six velocities, in doublings, runs 1.36 in pitch and 1.14 in decay for the toms, 3.43 in pitch and 3.05 in decay for the hats, 2.05 in level for the cymbals, 2.13 in decay for the congas, and 5.67 in decay for the triangle pair. The one family deliberately left out is the whistle pair, whose every relation sits at or under the floor - 0.31 in pitch and in decay, 0.18 in colour, 0.20 in level - and whose length is the 50 ms gate rather than the instrument, see `_stimulus`. A relation fitted to that fits the capture recipe.
_bandwidth: The two references do not have the same bandwidth, and the narrower one is the GM standard kit this capture is named for. Its highest 1/3-octave band still within 80 dB of its own peak sits at a median of 11.4 kHz across 25 diagnostic notes, against 22.8 kHz for the second reference on every one of them; at 14 kHz it reads 97 to 122 dB under its own peak and at 18 kHz, 125 to 152. A 16-bit recording's noise floor is about -96 dB, so that content was removed rather than rolled off, and the knee sits at the Nyquist of 22.05 kHz. Both come from the same plugin and the same rack through the same capture path, which is what says this belongs to the sample set and not to the harness. Two separate ceilings follow and `shared_band_edge` takes the narrower. Each reference on its own stops telling its instruments apart above 8 kHz - across the 47 instruments the interquartile spread of the band profile holds between 18 and 29 dB from 1 kHz to 8 kHz and is exactly 0.0 at 10 kHz and 12.5 kHz, where all 282 rows sit on the band floor. But discriminating is not the same as being right, and above 4 kHz these two do not agree about where the instruments are: the median offset between them wanders between -9 and +6 dB from 50 Hz to 4 kHz against an interquartile spread held near 12, then runs to -11.4, -17.5 and -24.4 dB at 5, 6.3 and 8 kHz while that spread does not move. A shift every instrument shares is a chain, not a kit, so the usable edge is 5 kHz rather than 8. What that is worth: cut there, the two references' disagreement about brightness falls from 1.92x to 1.09x, and the direction stops being one-sided - 93 percent of cells had read the second reference brighter, and 69 percent do now. Both sides of a comparison are measured with the edge applied - the band profile, the per-octave decay and the centroid's integration range alike - so a model with a real wash is neither charged for it nor allowed to normalise its whole profile against it. What this does NOT do is supply a target up there. Above 5 kHz this capture calibrates nothing, and a cymbal's identity is largely above it; a metallic residual in that region is unmeasured rather than measured and missed.
_velocities: Velocity is the only axis a drum note has, so the grid carries both the set a fit is scored on (64, 100, 127) and the set it is validated against (48, 88, 112) from the same capture. Rendering the holdout now is what makes the generalisation check free later; capturing only the fit set makes it impossible.
_dimensions:
A kit gets the percussion dimensions - band tilt, band profile error, per-octave decay, attack, crest, brightness, level, velocity range, ring length, tonality and image - because the pitched ones are built on a fundamental (the harmonic ladder, the intonation error, the tone-to-noise ratio) and a drum hit does not have one. All eleven are named rather than left empty, and the difference is what the list asserts: empty means 'whatever was measured', so a gate's bounds would be a byproduct of the measurement rather than a claim about what this kit is judged on, and a dimension that quietly stopped being produced would read as one fewer bound and nothing else. Named, the eleven are the denominator, and one that cannot be reached has to be argued in `dimensions_na` instead of vanishing - the same discipline the parity allowlist runs on. One is excused, and it is `stereo`; see `_dimensions_na`. The other ten carry a column in the reference profile for every row.

The last three exist because the eight before them are all read off a 1/3-octave profile or an envelope, and three qualities are structurally outside both. Every spectral column is a level or a first moment over those bands, so a comb of tones - one per band, each carrying that band's energy - has the same profile as the noise it was built from to a hundredth of a decibel, the same tilt and the same centroid, and nothing in the set could separate a struck bar from a filtered shaker. How long a hit lasts is not in a spectrum at all: `decay_ms` was measured from the first grid and compared by nothing, while `band_decay` - its nearest stand-in - averages only the octaves both sides resolved, so a hit that ends early loses those octaves from its own average instead of being charged for them. And an image is not in a mono mix. `ring` is the time to fall 20 dB in doublings rather than in milliseconds or percent, because the kit spans 24x on it (60 ms of woodblock against 1428 of cymbal) so a median in milliseconds is the cymbals, and percent prices a doubling at +100 and a halving at -50. `tonality` is spectral flatness over the first 300 ms, geometric mean over arithmetic, and it is a different measurement from the pitched set's `tnr_db` rather than the same one renamed: that one masks around a harmonic ladder and there is no ladder here. What it does NOT answer is how NARROW a peak is: a line and a filled quarter-octave carrying the same band energy come back about a decibel apart, which is inside the 3.50 dB the two references disagree by, so sharpness within a band is still unmeasured and a small `tonality` delta is not evidence about it. It is also the more trustworthy instrument on the metal - `measure_modes` returns twelve peaks for a cymbal and those peaks move by 14 percent of their frequency between velocities of the same instrument, so a mask built from them would be measuring the extractor. Measured across kit-a it separates the kit by 49 dB, from -55.6 to -6.8, in the order a listener would give: triangle -45.8, woodblock -28.1, claves -27.6, cowbell -22.7, kick -22.1, ride -17.2, conga -14.2, maracas -9.7, hats and snare -8.8, crash -8.0.

Which of them a gate can hold is a different question and was measured rather than judged: for each dimension, the spread of the delta across the six velocities of one instrument against the spread across the 47 instruments. A dimension where the first approaches the second is measuring the measurement. Taken as the ratio of the two: for each note the median absolute deviation of the delta across its six velocities, medianed over the 47, against the same deviation taken over the 47 per-note medians. Read once over the model's deltas against kit-a - band_shape 0.10, centroid_pct 0.20, band_tilt and attack 0.29, band_decay 0.36, crest 0.38, level 0.47 - and again, for the three added later, over the two REFERENCES' deltas against each other, which is the same arithmetic on a pair that does not move when the model does: stereo 0.08, band_decay 0.10, centroid_pct 0.15, band_tilt 0.16, ring 0.25, band_shape 0.30, tonality 0.31, level 0.33, attack 0.38, crest 0.47. The two readings do not have to agree and they broadly do; where they part - band_shape and band_decay swap ends - the reference pair is answering about two recordings and the model pair about one voice, so neither replaces the other. Every dimension separates instruments on both, and the closest to its own noise is whichever of crest and level the reading puts last, which is the one to distrust first if a gate on it starts failing on nothing. `stereo`'s 0.08 is the reading to distrust most, for the opposite reason: it separates perfectly because one reference is mono and the other is not, which is a fact about the two recordings rather than about 47 instruments. `vel_range` has no reading here and cannot have one: it is a span over the velocities, so one note yields one value and there is no within-note spread to take. What this does NOT say is that every note is measurable. It is a median over the kit, and two notes' attack readings swing across velocity by nearly their whole value - the chinese cymbal at 63 ms of spread on a 64 ms median with the reference itself swinging 40, and the open triangle at 15 on a 17.5 against a reference that holds to 0.5. Those two are decided by where a rippling envelope happens to cross the tolerance rather than by a rise time, so their magnitudes are not worth chasing; the china's is not measurable on either side. The references' own disagreement, by the same arithmetic the model goes through: band_decay 41.70 dB/s, centroid 21.00 percent, level 10.20 dB, band_shape 9.85 dB, band_tilt 6.06 dB, vel_range 4.16 dB, tonality 3.50 dB, attack 2.50 ms, crest 2.12 dB, ring 0.69 doublings. A kit's ring length is the loosest of them in proportion to its own range: 0.69 doublings is a factor of 1.6, so this gate catches a hit that is several times wrong and passes anything a second real kit could have been.
_dimensions_na: `stereo` is the one percussion dimension this capture cannot supply, and it is excused from the reference rather than from the instrument: a kit has an image, and the second reference has one - `stereo_width` runs 0.008 to 0.999 across kit-b with a median of 0.710. kit-a does not. Its two channels are bit-identical on every one of the 282 rows (max |L-R| 5.5e-12, which is the float arithmetic), so the width is exactly 0.000 throughout. A bound recorded from it would hold the model to a mono kit, and 38 of libsonare's drum notes carry a `stereo_spread` that would then be fitted to zero. Recorded here rather than left out of the dimension list, because the gap is real and belongs in coverage: the kit's image is unmeasured against this reference and stays unmeasured until kit-b or another capture is the one the gate reads.

dimensions_na.stereo: the reference kit renders dual mono: kit-a's two channels are bit-identical on all 282 rows, so the width is zero by construction rather than by voicing. The second reference is genuinely wide (median 0.710), so this is an absence in the timbre the gate is recorded against and not in the instrument

_identity: Which product this is captured from lives in the untracked sibling `drums.local.json`: the plugin's component triple and each timbre's preset. Everything here is the method. Re-capturing needs the overlay; scoring and fitting read the rendered corpus and need nothing.
